lesson.title: Teratogens: How Timing Turns Exposure Into Harm
lesson.summary: Teratogens are outside agents, drugs, chemicals, infections, or other environmental factors, that can disrupt normal prenatal development, and how much harm they cause depends heavily on timing, dose, and the individual fetus.
lesson.body:
A teratogen is anything from outside the developing organism, a substance, an infection, or a form of radiation, that can interfere with normal prenatal development and increase the risk of birth defects or developmental problems. The word comes from the Greek for "monster-forming," reflecting how this area of research originally grew out of studying visible birth defects, though today the field also studies more subtle effects on brain and behavioral development.

Timing matters enormously. As the prenatal development chapter explained, the embryonic stage is when major organs and structures are first being formed, so exposure during that narrow window tends to cause the most severe structural damage. The same teratogen, at the same dose, can have a very different effect during the fetal stage, when organs already exist and are mainly growing and maturing rather than forming from scratch.

Alcohol is the most thoroughly documented behavioral teratogen. Prenatal alcohol exposure can cause fetal alcohol spectrum disorders, which range in severity and can include distinctive facial features, growth deficits, and lasting effects on attention, learning, and impulse control. No amount of prenatal alcohol exposure has been established as clearly safe, which is why health guidelines generally recommend avoiding alcohol entirely during pregnancy.

Other well documented teratogens include nicotine, which is associated with lower birth weight, certain medications and illegal drugs, and some maternal infections. Rubella (German measles) contracted early in pregnancy is a classic example from the history of this research, since it can cause deafness, cataracts, and heart defects in the developing baby. Heavy metals such as lead and mercury and certain forms of radiation are also known risks.

It is important not to treat teratogen research as deterministic. Not every fetus exposed to a given teratogen is affected, and not all affected fetuses are affected equally. Dose, timing, duration of exposure, and the genetic makeup of both mother and fetus all influence the outcome, which is why researchers talk about increased risk and probability rather than certainty.
